title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins (anthropic.com)
comments: While this confirms the method of production it doesn't say anything about their selection, especially since they were, apparently, generated over a period of months. Specifically you cannot see those candidates that were generated and discarded."It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator."Yes."However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated."Does not logically follow when "doing and saying nothing" will completely suffice.reply

Given how expensive this computation would have been in 1997, it makes perfect sense they'd taken months, but even if we assume they tried all timestamps of 1997 and selected arbitrarily among the first 16 viable candidate of any timestamp, that's just ~30 bits of freedom.Finding out there is a class of weak 256-bit elliptic curves so large that they can be hit randomly with 2^30 tries would be a cryptanalytic breakthrough analogous to discovering all elliptic curve cryptography is broken.Read section 3.1 of the Koblitz and Menezes paper. It was already implausible with 160 bits of freedom. https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/1018If you want to believe the NSA knows ECC is broken and chose to risk moving the US government to it and somehow no one figured out the same break in 30 years, you're free to do so. But pretending the seed choice plays any role in that theory is over.reply

This is unrelated to the above comment, but I figured I'd ask while we're here. You state at the end of your blog post on this topic that you'd now probably recommend the NIST curves over Curve25519. Why is that?reply
As a complete layman, I do wonder why n grows with each subsequent curve, rather than with number of bits. Does this not suggest they were 'searching harder'?reply

Almost all of the smaller values of n are not valid curve values, so they were searching "harder" but just for valid seeds. If you look at the generator output in [1], you'll see that:1. Only a very small number of valid seeds were discarded when compared to the number of n values. It seems we don't yet know why about half of the valid seeds were discarded but the explanation of a buggy curve validity checker doesn't seem implausible to me.2. Directly to your point, most of the prime192 and prime239 curves required larger n values to find a valid seed and they are both smaller and used an earlier timestamp.[1]: https://words.filippo.io/seeds-solved/reply
>they can be hit randomly with 2^30 triesMore precisely: not very random tries.reply

unless your guess is that the hypothetical ECC weakness is somehow correlated with the LCG structure, the draws from the LCG are as good as random.It is possible such a correlation could occur. but it would be much weirder than this being the result of a random search, which would already be very weird.reply

I find it slightly less weird because I see potential for indirect attacks on the not-quite-so-ECC parts of actual implementations. Wherever a network client can ask many times for each of the different, but somehow not entirely uncorrelated curves, it might be able to expose previously not deemed critical side channels. Following in the general direction of the discoveries that so far resulted in IV and padding determinism/randomness being considered as important as the "actual crypto" itself. In that case the structures that would need to somehow interact would not be ECC and LCG, but merely LCG and key derivation..reply
"..chose to risk moving the US government to it.."Oof, about that...reply
go on...reply

first_paragraph:
Every layer is a memory store[code][interactive app]Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world.
Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium.
It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again.
We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to.

comments: I always found the difference between ham radio operators and computer hacker community interesting.There is obvious large overlap. Both are nerdy and techy and attract similar base groups. But the ham space is dominated by people who want to be "good citizens" through collective action, while computer hacker is more about cyberpunk "if I could do it, then it's allowed".Perhaps it's the clearest example of "The medium is the message" concept.reply

It is very strange that when you come across anything radio related, people seemingly come out of the woodwork to tell you not that you are necessarily, actively doing something against regulation, but that there is always potential to be breaking the law.Take this Hackaday article from the other day:https://hackaday.com/2026/10/15/so-you-want-to-make-your-sdr...The subject is mostly academic, but in 18 comments no less than 3 different people are warning about doing something against the rules. It's weird. I don't know of any other subject that provokes responses about "the rules" like this.
I could understand if the article title was "How to Aim Laser Pointers at Airplanes", but attach a long enough wire to an oscillator and people start to get uppity.On the other side of things, I don't know if you've turned on a shortwave radio recently, but the only thing I hear on mine is switch-mode power supply noise.reply

Hams take pride in being largely self-policing because this is one of the things that keeps the FCC interested in reserving sections of the spectrum for ham use.Also, I love hackaday for their articles but the comment section there is among the worst on the Internet. You'll find more enlightening discussions on the wall of a truckstop bathroom stall.reply

Like I said, "The medium is the message"One bad transmitter in your neighborhood can cut you off from the hobby. Someone who's into linux and computers can follow an online tutorial to rig together an SDR. Look at a bunch of numbers or static, shrug and move on to a different project without disconnecting that anttena breaking an entire band for all of his neighbors. Then it's on those neighbors to go build a directional antenna and buy portable radio gear and then do their own "in the field investigation" to isolate which house is doing that, then go try to explain to the random person they are polluting a band and hope the person is friendly and cooperative.In a perfect world the FCC would do that, but getting the FCC to act on small infractions like that is a slow and long process and often goes unanswered. Especially if you're not near a marina or a federal building or an airport. So one hackaday reader can take down ham operation in an entire area because they were just interested in a weekend DIY project.People throw that "against the law" to limit the damage. But actually getting the FCC to prosecute these issues is a challenge in itself.reply

first of all, you can only broadcast "on top" of something if you're using an AM mode, and even then who wants to be talking through a spurious signal? Would you wanna have random voices or other sounds played over a phone call, interrupting conversation?Why are you rationalizing / defending categorically anti-social behavior?reply

There are power regulations. You can't simply broadcast a more powerful signal. And that also only makes the problem worse for everyone else, it immediately turns into a room of people shouting over each other and nothing actually being communicated.And you cannot simply switch bands, because amateur bands are very specific.You're left with attempting some form of recoverable signal modulation which can propagate through the problem area, but it becomes akin to making ripples in a turbulent river. The ripples simply do not contain the energy to resist diffusion of the surrounding heat in the environment for any considerable length of time. We definitely have techniques for propagating multiple signals across the same frequency band, it's fundamental to modern communication, but it still comes with physical limitations.reply

comments: This builds on the Kickmix quantum language from Google. title: C++26: The New Debugging Header (sandordargo.com)
comments: Sadly the PR gets a detail wrong:> Implementations are expected to optimize the code generated to be as minimal as possible for the platform. For example, on X86 it’s expected that this produces a single INT3 instruction. The goal in this expectation is to place the debugger as close as possible in the caller of breakpoint() to improve the debugging experience for users.This is the wrong design on x86 at least with many debuggers. x86’s int3 is a trap and reports the address of the next instruction in the saved register state [0]. Most debuggers are not very clever and just use the saved address to generate the offending line of code and the call stack. But if the trap sequence is just int3, then the saved address could be outside the offending basic block or even outside the function entirely. gdb is certainly in the class of debuggers that get this wrong.The easy workaround is to generate int3; nop for the breakpoint instead of just int3. The saved address will point to the nop and the debugger will be happy.[0] FRED also reports the instruction length, allowing one to deduce the trapping address.reply

I don't see how this happens in a C++ function, since breakpoint() is not noreturn you'd have to be doing something very strange for the next instruction to be outside the function. It's possible some debuggers will show the next line, and even then that seems like a debugger QoL issue that's fixable pretty mechanically. A soft breakpoint can come from CD 3 or CC, even if you don't get the instruction length from the CPU there aren't that many possibilities. I'm sure we don't need everyone to start inserting extra NOPs to get the desired behavior.reply

Boost.Test has debugger_break(), Catch2 has CATCH_BREAK_INTO_DEBUGGER, Dear ImGui has IM_DEBUG_BREAK() and Unreal has UE_DEBUG_BREAK. The platform knowledge required is arcane but well-known to tooling implementers — it just wasn’t standardized.C++26 fixes this with P2546R5 and its companion P2810R4 thanks to Rene Ferdinand Rivera Morell.
